lead: Energy is conserved; entropy is not. In every real process the total entropy of the system plus its surroundings rises, and the amount it rises by is the entropy generated, S<sub>gen</sub>. This one inequality decides which processes are possible, separates the best possible machine from the actual one, and shows where a plant is destroying quality of energy. Engineers use it to judge heat exchanger designs, steam plant performance and any claim of a new, super-efficient engine.
prereq: You need: entropy as a property for dS = δQrev/T, and reversible and irreversible processes for what makes a process irreversible.

sections.h3: The principle written as an equation

blocks.text: For any process between state 1 and state 2, reversible or not, the entropy account reads as follows.

ΔSsystem + ΔSsurroundings = Sgen ≥ 0
ΔSsystem is the entropy change of the system in kJ/K, equal to S₂ − S₁; ΔSsurroundings is the entropy change of everything outside the system, in kJ/K; Sgen is the entropy generated during the process, in kJ/K; the sum is never negative.

The equality holds only for a fully reversible process. Every real process gives a strict greater-than. S<sub>gen</sub> is not a property of the system; it is a quantity produced along the path, and it depends on how the process is carried out.

Seal the system and its surroundings into one box and you have an isolated system. For it the statement becomes: the entropy of an isolated system increases in every real process and stays constant only in a reversible one. It never falls. That is the second law stated in entropy words.

Compare this with the first law. The first law says energy is conserved, so the energy account always balances to zero. The second law says the entropy account does not balance to zero — it always leaves a positive remainder. Nature keeps books that never close.

sections.h3: S<sub>gen</sub> measures how irreversible the process is

blocks.text: S<sub>gen</sub> is a quantitative measure of irreversibility. Large S<sub>gen</sub> means a badly irreversible process; zero means a reversible one. Four sources account for almost every case you will meet.
Heat through a finite temperature difference is the commonest. When Q kilojoules cross from a body at T<sub>hot</sub> to a body at T<sub>cold</sub>, both in kelvin:

Sgen = Q (1/Tcold − 1/Thot)
Q is the heat in kJ passing from the hot body to the cold body; Tcold and Thot are in K; Sgen is in kJ/K. The bracket is positive because Tcold < Thot, so a wider gap or a larger Q creates more entropy.

blocks.text: A reversible adiabatic process has Q = 0 and no friction or mixing, so S<sub>gen</sub> = 0 and ΔS = 0. Such a process is called isentropic — same entropy. On a T-s diagram the ideal gas turbine or compressor is drawn as a vertical line.

sections.h3: The criterion for a spontaneous change

blocks.text: The same inequality answers a different question: will this change happen on its own? For a closed system held at constant internal energy U and constant volume V, with no help from outside, the answer is yes only if dS ≥ 0. Entropy climbs to a maximum, and that maximum is the equilibrium state.

Only a few universities ask for this form. At constant temperature and volume the criterion is written with the Helmholtz function, and at constant temperature and pressure with the Gibbs function; both belong to the topic of Gibbs and Helmholtz functions.

A positive ΔS says the process can happen, not that it happens quickly. The conversion of diamond to graphite has a positive ΔS at room conditions and you will not see it happen in your lifetime. Thermodynamics gives direction, never rate.

Every kJ/K of entropy generated makes T₀ × Sgen of work unavailable, where T₀ is the temperature of the surroundings in K. This lost work, Wlost = T₀Sgen, is the Gouy-Stodola relation; the topic of available energy turns it into exergy, the part of energy still useful. For flowing streams the same account is written per second in entropy generation in control volumes.

examples.question: In an insulated vessel, 2 kg of water at 80 °C is mixed with 3 kg of water at 20 °C. Take cp = 4.187 kJ/kg·K and treat it as constant. Find the final mixture temperature and the total entropy change, and state whether the mixing is reversible. (8 marks)
steps: Convert to kelvin: T₁ = 80 + 273 = 353 K, T₂ = 20 + 273 = 293 K.

The vessel is insulated and no work crosses the boundary, so the heat given up by the hot water equals the heat taken by the cold water: m₁cp(T₁ − T<sub>f</sub>) = m₂cp(T<sub>f</sub> − T₂). The cp cancels.
Entropy change of the hot water: ΔS₁ = m₁cp ln(T<sub>f</sub>/T₁) = 2 × 4.187 × ln(317/353) = 8.374 × (−0.10757) = −0.9008 kJ/K.
Entropy change of the cold water: ΔS₂ = m₂cp ln(T<sub>f</sub>/T₂) = 3 × 4.187 × ln(317/293) = 12.561 × (0.07873) = +0.9889 kJ/K.
The vessel is insulated, so the surroundings change by zero. Total: ΔS<sub>total</sub> = −0.9008 + 0.9889 = +0.0882 kJ/K = S<sub>gen</sub>.
The total is positive, so the mixing is irreversible and allowed by the second law. Warm water giving heat to cold water is exactly the finite-temperature-gap source of entropy.
examples.answer: Final temperature 317 K (44 °C) and total entropy change +0.0882 kJ/K; positive, so the mixing is irreversible and possible.
examples.check:
import math
m1, T1 = 2.0, 353.0
m2, T2 = 3.0, 293.0
cp = 4.187
Tf = (m1*T1 + m2*T2)/(m1 + m2)
dS1 = m1*cp*math.log(Tf/T1)
dS2 = m2*cp*math.log(Tf/T2)
print(round(Tf, 2))
print(round(dS1, 4))
print(round(dS2, 4))
print(round(dS1 + dS2, 4))

traps: ΔS of the system alone may be negative — freezing water and compressing gas both do it. Only system plus surroundings is guaranteed non-negative, so write the full account before you conclude anything.
S<sub>gen</sub> is in kJ/K, not kJ. Dividing Q by a temperature in °C gives nonsense; convert to kelvin first.
A reversible adiabatic process is isentropic (ΔS = 0). A reversible isothermal process is not: ΔS = Q/T is finite. Do not label every reversible process isentropic.
When the vessel is not insulated, the surroundings' entropy change must be added with its sign. Many answers lose marks by silently dropping it.
A positive ΔS says the process can happen, not that it happens quickly. Direction comes from thermodynamics; rate comes from kinetics.

quiz.q: State the principle of increase of entropy as one equation and define every term with its unit.
quiz.a: ΔS<sub>system</sub> + ΔS<sub>surroundings</sub> = S<sub>gen</sub> ≥ 0, all in kJ/K: ΔS<sub>system</sub> = S₂ − S₁ of the system, ΔS<sub>surroundings</sub> the change of everything outside it, and S<sub>gen</sub> the entropy created, which is zero only for a reversible process.

quiz.q: For which kind of process is S<sub>gen</sub> exactly zero?
quiz.a: A fully reversible process. A reversible adiabatic process also has ΔS = 0 and is called isentropic.

quiz.q: Water in a freezer loses entropy as it turns to ice. Does this break the second law?
quiz.a: No. The freezer's refrigerant and compressor reject more entropy to the room than the water loses. ΔS<sub>water</sub> + ΔS<sub>surroundings</sub> > 0; only the total is protected.

quiz.q: 50 kJ of heat flows from a body at 400 K to a body at 300 K. Find the entropy generated.
1 kg of water at 90 °C is mixed with 2 kg at 30 °C in an insulated vessel. Take cp = 4.187 kJ/kg·K. Find the final temperature and the total entropy change.
A gas is compressed isothermally from 100 kPa to 500 kPa and ΔS of the gas is negative. A student claims the second law is violated. What is missing from the argument?
quiz.a: The system's entropy may fall. Work is supplied and heat is rejected to the surroundings, whose entropy rises by at least as much. Check ΔS<sub>sys</sub> + ΔS<sub>surr</sub> = S<sub>gen</sub> ≥ 0; for a reversible isothermal compression S<sub>gen</sub> = 0 and the total is exactly zero.

quiz.q: 100 kJ leaves a 500 K body. In case A it goes directly to a 300 K body. In case B a reversible engine works between the same two bodies and the same 100 kJ leaves the hot body. Compare the entropy generated.
quiz.a: Direct: S<sub>gen</sub> = 100(1/300 − 1/500) = 0.1333 kJ/K. With the reversible engine S<sub>gen</sub> = 0, because Q<sub>h</sub>/T<sub>h</sub> = Q<sub>c</sub>/T<sub>c</sub> and there is no friction; part of the 100 kJ leaves as work, so less heat reaches the cold body. Case A generates 0.1333 kJ/K; with the surroundings at 300 K that is 300 × 0.1333 = 40 kJ of work lost, exactly the work the reversible engine of case B delivers, 100 × (1 − 300/500) = 40 kJ.

quiz.q: Why is a reversible adiabatic process called isentropic?
quiz.a: Because δQ = 0 and there is no internal irreversibility, so ΔS = ∫δQ<sub>rev</sub>/T = 0. Entropy stays constant: iso (same) + entropic (entropy).

beyond: Not for the exam. In plant practice, S<sub>gen</sub> is the number behind second law efficiency and exergy audits: a boiler that creates 2 kJ/K per kg of steam is throwing away work that a better-matched heat exchanger could recover. Modern curricula add entropy generation minimisation and the Bejan number to design heat exchangers and solar collectors. Researchers apply the same inequality to living systems and to data centres, where engineers now report the entropy generated, in J/K, alongside the waste heat itself. Search for entropy generation number, Gouy-Stodola theorem and exergy destruction to go further.
